hook.situation: You are in a clothing store, want to try on a shirt, ask for a different size, choose something neat for an interview, and check whether exchange or refund is possible.
objectives: Use clothing words with 입다, 신다, 사이즈가 맞다, and 잘 어울리다.
Ask store staff politely with 입어 봐도 돼요? and 보여 주시겠어요?
Describe appearance and interview appropriateness with 커 보여요, 단정해 보여요, and N보다 더 A.
hook.whyItMatters: This chapter should not be a random clothing list. The vocabulary has to serve one real flow: try on clothes, judge fit and style, compare options, and confirm store policy before buying.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 보세요 — Try doing it
grammarNotes.func: Suggest that the listener try an action to see how it goes — perfect for inviting someone to try a piece of clothing on, try a color, or give a style a go. It softens a plain command into friendly encouragement: go ahead and try it.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in ㅏ or ㅗ
Verb stem ends in any other vowel or a consonant
formTable.ex: 입다 → 입어 보세요 (try wearing it), 신다 → 신어 보세요 (try them on)
착용하다 → 착용해 보세요 (try wearing it on)

examples.en: Try this dress on.
examples.note: 한번 (once / give it a go) commonly pairs with -아/어 보세요 to mean a light, no-pressure try.

examples.en: Try this hat on too.
examples.note: 쓰다 (to wear on the head) is a ㅡ-irregular: ㅡ drops before -어, giving 써 보세요.

examples.en: Try these shoes on.
examples.note: 신다 = to wear on the feet. Each clothing verb is different, but all combine the same way with 보세요.

examples.en: Try picking the red one.
examples.note: 고르다 is a 르-irregular, so 고르 → 골라 before -아; you are inviting them to try choosing.

keyPoint.label: -(으)세요 vs -아/어 보세요
keyPoint.body: 입으세요 = Put it on (a plain polite command). 입어 보세요 = Try it on (and see) — it adds the nuance of testing or experiencing, which is why a shop clerk says 입어 보세요, not 입으세요.

drill.instruction: Invite the customer to try each item, using V-아/어 보세요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English try on makes learners reach for a word meaning try/attempt (시도하다). In Korean you keep the real clothing verb (입다/신다/쓰다) and just attach 보세요; the try meaning comes entirely from 보세요.

grammarNotes.title: V-아/어 주시겠어요? — Could you please do it for me?
grammarNotes.func: A very polite request asking someone to do something for your benefit. In a shop or fitting room it is how you ask the clerk to bring another size, show you a color, or give you a hand. -주다 adds for me, and -시겠어요? makes it gentle and respectful.

formTable.ex: 찾다 → 찾아 주시겠어요? (could you find it for me?)

formTable.when: Stem ends in another vowel or consonant
formTable.ex: 보이다 → 보여 주시겠어요? (could you show me?)
추천하다 → 추천해 주시겠어요? (could you recommend one?)

examples.en: Could you bring me a bigger size?
examples.note: 가져다주다 (bring for someone) is the go-to fitting-room request; -주시겠어요? keeps it polite to the clerk.

examples.en: Could you show me another color too?
examples.note: 보이다 → 보여; 보여 주다 literally show for me, the natural way to ask to be shown an item.

examples.en: Could you find this shirt for me?
examples.note: 좀 softens the request even more — a near-obligatory politeness word in spoken requests.

examples.ko: 이 바지 잘 어울리는지 봐 주시겠어요?
examples.romanization: i baji jal eoullineunji bwa jusigesseoyo?
examples.en: Could you check whether these pants suit me?
examples.note: 보다 → 봐; asking someone to look or check for your benefit, a common appearance question to a friend or clerk.

keyPoint.label: -아/어 주세요 vs -아/어 주시겠어요?
keyPoint.body: 가져다 주세요 = Please bring it (polite request). 가져다 주시겠어요? = Could you bring it? — the -시겠어요? question form is one step more deferential and indirect, the safest choice with a stranger or staff.

drill.instruction: Make each request polite using V-아/어 주시겠어요?
items: 작은 사이즈 / 찾다 (write: 작은 사이즈 찾아 주시겠어요?)
이 옷 / 추천하다 (write: 이 옷 추천해 주시겠어요?)

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 더 큰 사이즈로 가져다 주시겠어요 나를 위해?
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners add for me as a separate phrase (나를 위해) by analogy with English. The benefit is already built into 주다, so adding 나를 위해 is redundant and unnatural — just use 주시겠어요?.

grammarNotes.title: A-아/어 보이다 — It looks / appears
grammarNotes.func: Describe how something or someone appears to the observer. Attached to an adjective it means looks (pretty/big/expensive); it is the everyday way to compliment an outfit or comment on how clothes look on someone.

formTable.when: Stem ends in another vowel or consonant

examples.en: That dress really looks pretty.
examples.note: 예쁘다 → 예뻐 (ㅡ drops before -어); the headline example for this pattern.

examples.en: This coat looks a bit expensive.
examples.note: 비싸다 ends in ㅏ, so the -아 merges in: 비싸 보여요; commenting on apparent price.

examples.en: That color looks like it suits you well.
examples.note: 어울리다 → 어울려; pairing 잘 어울리다 with 보이다 is the standard it looks good on you comment.

examples.ko: 이 신발을 신으니까 키가 커 보여요.
examples.romanization: i sinbareul sineunikka kiga keo boyeoyo.
examples.en: With these shoes on, you look taller.
examples.note: 크다 → 커; appearance changes caused by clothing are exactly what -아/어 보이다 expresses.

keyPoint.label: 예뻐요 vs 예뻐 보여요
keyPoint.body: 예뻐요 = It is pretty (your judgment of the thing itself). 예뻐 보여요 = It looks pretty (how it appears, possibly more than it really is). Use 보이다 when you are describing an impression or the effect an outfit gives.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 보여요 is pronounced with a smooth y-glide [bo-yeo-yo]; learners often clip it to [bo-eo-yo] — keep the ㅕ. In 좋아 보여요, ㅎ is silent before a vowel, so 좋아 links as [jo-a].

drill.instruction: Say how each looks using A-아/어 보여요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English looks like it is pretty tempts learners to build a heavy ~것처럼 보이다 clause. For a simple adjective impression, Korean just fuses the adjective with 보이다: 예뻐 보여요.

grammarNotes.title: A-(으)ㄴ N — An adjective before a noun
grammarNotes.func: Turn a descriptive adjective into a modifier that sits directly in front of a noun — the basic way to say a pretty dress, a long skirt, black shoes. Essential for describing clothing and appearance with detail.

formTable.when: Adjective stem ends in a vowel
Adjective stem ends in a consonant

examples.en: I like long skirts.
examples.note: 길다 is a ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops and -ㄴ attaches → 긴. A classic irregular to flag for clothing length.

examples.en: I wore black dress shoes.
examples.note: 검다 → 검은; consonant-final stems take -은. 검은색 (black color) is everyday clothing vocabulary.

examples.en: This is a small hat.
examples.note: 작다 → 작은; the modifier comes directly before the noun with no extra particle — unlike English, no is needed.

examples.en: I bought new sneakers.
examples.note: 새 (new) is a determiner that takes no ending at all — a common exception worth memorizing alongside the rule.

keyPoint.label: 치마가 길어요 vs 긴 치마
keyPoint.body: 치마가 길어요 = The skirt is long (adjective as predicate, sentence-final). 긴 치마 = a long skirt (adjective modifying the noun, mid-sentence). The same adjective takes -아/어요 to end a sentence but -(으)ㄴ to sit before a noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 작은 links as [ja-geun] — the final ㄱ of 작 moves onto the -은 (resyllabification). Likewise 검은 → [geo-meun], 좋은 → [jo-eun] (ㅎ silent).

drill.instruction: Combine the adjective and noun into A-(으)ㄴ N.
items: 하얗다 + 셔츠 (write: 하얀 셔츠 — ㅎ-irregular: ㅎ drops)
멋있다 + 코트 (write: 멋있는 코트 — 있다 type takes -는)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: With ㄹ-irregular adjectives like 길다, learners try to add -은 to a stem that already kept ㄹ. Instead the ㄹ drops and only -ㄴ attaches: 길다 → 긴 치마, not 길은/긴은 치마.

grammarNotes.title: N보다 (더) — More ... than N
grammarNotes.func: Compare two things: mark the standard of comparison (the thing you measure against) with 보다, and add 더 (more) for emphasis. Ideal for clothing and appearance — saying one skirt is longer than another, or one coat is more expensive than another.

formTable.when: After any noun (the thing compared against)
formTable.ex: 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요 (this skirt is longer than that one)

formTable.when: Add 더 before the adjective for emphasis
formTable.ex: 이 코트가 저 코트보다 더 비싸요 (this coat is more expensive than that one)
이 신발이 저 신발보다 덜 편해요 (these shoes are less comfortable than those)

examples.en: This dress is prettier than that one.
examples.note: 보다 attaches to 저 원피스, the thing being compared against — no separate word for than is needed.

examples.ko: 검은색 구두가 흰색보다 더 잘 어울려요.
examples.romanization: geomeunsaek guduga huinsaekboda deo jal eoullyeoyo.
examples.en: Black shoes suit you better than white ones.
examples.note: 더 (more) plus 잘 어울리다 is the natural way to say something suits you better.

examples.en: These pants are shorter than those.
examples.note: 짧다 → 짧아요; comparing length is a very common clothing comment.

examples.ko: 이 모자가 저 모자보다 더 커요.
examples.romanization: i mojaga jeo mojaboda deo keoyo.
examples.en: This hat is bigger than that one.
examples.note: 크다 → 커요; 더 reinforces the comparison but the sentence is already comparative thanks to 보다.

keyPoint.label: Where 보다 attaches
keyPoint.body: 보다 attaches to the standard (the thing you measure against), not the subject. 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요 = this skirt is longer than that skirt. The 가-marked noun is the winner; the 보다-marked noun is what it beats.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 보다 is always pronounced [bo-da] and attaches directly with no space in writing: 저 치마보다. 더 [deo] is a separate word with a clear ㅓ vowel — do not reduce it to [deu].

drill.instruction: Make a comparison with N보다 (더) using the cue.
drill.model: 이 치마 / 저 치마 / 길다 → 이 치마가 저 치마보다 길어요.
items: 이 코트 / 저 코트 / 비싸다 (write: 이 코트가 저 코트보다 비싸요.)
이 신발 / 저 신발 / 더 편하다 (write: 이 신발이 저 신발보다 더 편해요.)
빨간색 / 파란색 / 잘 어울리다 (write: 빨간색이 파란색보다 잘 어울려요.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts than that one at the end, so learners tack 저 치마보다 on after the adjective. In Korean the 보다 phrase must come before the adjective: subject + 보다-phrase + 더 + adjective.

exampleSentence.en: May I try on this shirt?
I often wear T-shirts in summer.
The pants look a little big.
These dress shoes go well with the skirt.

exampleSentence.ko: 이 원피스는 면접에는 조금 화려해 보여요.
exampleSentence.en: This dress looks a little flashy for an interview.
May I try on these sneakers too?

exampleSentence.ko: 면접에는 운동화보다 구두가 더 단정해 보여요.
exampleSentence.en: For an interview, dress shoes look more presentable than sneakers.
Could you show me another color too?
For an interview, a navy shirt looks neat and presentable.

exampleSentence.ko: 사이즈가 조금 커서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
exampleSentence.en: The size is a little big, so could you show me one size smaller too?

exampleSentence.ko: 한 치수 작은 것도 입어 봐도 돼요?
exampleSentence.en: May I try on one size smaller too?
The fitting room is on the right.

extendedVocabulary.english: to suit; to look good on

exampleSentence.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-1971 and expression expr-765.

exampleSentence.en: Can I get a refund too?
exampleSentence.note: Linked to dictionary card word-ext-143 and expression expr-764.

exampleSentence.en: For an interview, a neat shirt is good.

extendedDialogue.setting: A shopper tries on a shirt, asks for another size, and chooses an interview outfit.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.en: May I try on this shirt?
lines.grammarNote: -아/어 봐도 돼요 asks permission to try an action.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.en: Yes, the fitting room is on the right.
lines.grammarNote: 피팅룸 is the store-location word connected to trying on.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 조금 커 보여요. 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
lines.romanization: jogeum keo boyeoyo. han chisu jageun geotdo boyeo jusigesseoyo?
lines.en: It looks a little big. Could you show me one size smaller too?
lines.grammarNote: 커 보여요 is appearance; 한 치수 작은 거 is the size request.

lines.speaker: 직원
lines.ko: 네. 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보여요.
lines.romanization: ne. myeonjeobeneun i syeocheuboda namsaek syeocheuga deo danjeonghae boyeoyo.
lines.en: Sure. For an interview, the navy shirt looks neater than this shirt.
lines.grammarNote: 이 셔츠보다 gives the comparison baseline, and 더 단정해 보여요 describes the appearance.

lines.speaker: 손님
lines.ko: 그럼 이걸로 할게요. 교환이나 환불도 돼요?
lines.romanization: geureom igeollo halgeyo. gyohwanina hwanbuldo dwaeyo?
lines.en: Then I'll take this one. Can I exchange or refund it too?
lines.grammarNote: 교환/환불이 되다 asks about store policy.

readingText.title: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
readingText.body: 민서는 면접에 입을 셔츠를 사러 갔어요. 먼저 직원에게 '이 셔츠 입어 봐도 돼요?'라고 물었어요. 피팅룸에서 입어 보니 사이즈가 조금 커 보였어요. 그래서 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 달라고 했어요. 직원은 면접에는 이 셔츠보다 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 보인다고 말했어요. 민서는 그 셔츠가 잘 어울리고 사이즈도 맞아서 샀어요. 마지막으로 교환이나 환불이 되는지도 확인했어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Minseo went to buy a shirt for an interview. First, Minseo asked a staff member if trying on the shirt was allowed. After trying it on in the fitting room, the size looked a little big, so Minseo asked to see one size smaller. The staff member said a navy shirt looked neater for an interview. It suited Minseo and the size fit, so Minseo bought it. Finally, Minseo checked whether exchange or refund was possible.

culturalNote.title: Fit, style, and policy are separate questions
culturalNote.body: In a Korean clothing store, keep three questions separate. First, size: 사이즈가 맞아요? 한 치수 작은 거 있어요? Second, style: 잘 어울려요? 단정해 보여요? Third, policy: 교환돼요? 환불돼요? Learners often mix these because English can say 'it works' for all three, but Korean uses different verbs.
culturalNote.tip: For clothes, 입다 is for clothing and 신다 is for shoes. For compliments, the clothing or color is the subject: 이 옷이 잘 어울려요, not 이 옷을 잘 어울려요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks permission to try on a shirt?
inlineExercises.explanation: 입다 is for clothing, and -아/어 봐도 돼요? asks permission.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence asks for one size smaller most deferentially?
options: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주세요.
한 치수 작은 것도 잘 어울려요?
inlineExercises.correct: 한 치수 작은 것도 보여 주시겠어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: Both 보여 주세요 and 보여 주시겠어요? are polite; the indirect -주시겠어요? form is more deferential.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence is about style, not size?
inlineExercises.explanation: 어울리다 describes whether something suits someone. 맞다 is about fit.

inlineExercises.prompt: Complete: 면접에는 남색 셔츠가 더 단정해 ___.
셔츠___ 입어 봐도 돼요? (May I try on the shirt?)
inlineExercises.explanation: 입다 takes the clothing item as an object, so 셔츠를 fits. 가 would make the shirt the subject.
-아/어 봐도 돼요? asks whether it is okay to try doing something. 입다 becomes 입어 봐도 돼요?

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'Could you show me a smaller size?'
inlineExercises.correct: 한 사이즈 작은 거 보여 주시겠어요?
inlineExercises.explanation: 작은 거 describes the smaller item you want. -주시겠어요? is a polite staff-facing request.
잘 어울려요 comments on style or fit with the person. It is not about the physical size being correct.
Shoes use 신다, not 입다. 입다 is for clothes worn on the body like shirts or coats.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “It looks too big”?
inlineExercises.explanation: -아/어 보이다 describes how something appears. 커 보여요 is the natural “looks big.”

bullets: Core flow: try on clothing, ask for another size, compare appearance, then check exchange/refund.
Use 입다 for clothes and 신다 for shoes.
맞다 is size fit, 어울리다 is style harmony, and 단정해 보이다 is presentable appearance.
Use 보여 주시겠어요? for polite staff requests and N보다 더 A for comparing options.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short message to a shop clerk while trying on clothes: compliment a color, ask for another size, and compare two items.
writingTask.hint: Use A-아/어 보이다 to say how it looks, A-(으)ㄴ N for the adjective+noun, N보다 (더) to compare, and V-아/어 주시겠어요? to ask politely.
writingTask.model: 이 남색 코트가 정말 따뜻해 보여요. 이 코트가 저 코트보다 더 예뻐요. 한 사이즈 작은 옷을 보여 주시겠어요?
writingTask.modelEn: This navy coat looks really warm. This coat is prettier than that coat. Could you show me a size smaller?

canDo: Invite someone to try something on (한번 입어 보세요)
Ask a clerk politely for help (다른 사이즈를 보여 주시겠어요?)
Say how clothes or a person look (따뜻해 보여요, 예뻐 보여요)
Put a descriptive adjective before a noun (예쁜 치마, 긴 바지)
Compare two items (이 옷이 저 옷보다 더 좋아요)
